title: Statistics - Lesson 2: Representative Data Assessment
description: Checkpoint on representative data, sampling bias, and evidence-based conclusions.

questions.question: A headline says, "Most students in the school want more project days." What is the population named in the claim?
options: All students in the school
Only students who like projects
Only the students surveyed
Only Grade 10 students
questions.explanation: The claim says students in the school, so the population is all students in the school.

questions.question: A researcher randomly selects 10 learners from each Grade 10 section. Which method is this closest to?
options: Stratified sampling
Voluntary response sampling
Convenience sampling
Asking friends
questions.explanation: The sample is taken from each section, which treats the sections as important subgroups.

questions.question: A voluntary response poll may overrepresent people with strong opinions.
questions.explanation: People with strong feelings are often more likely to choose to respond.

questions.question: A sample includes 75 learners, and 45 support the proposal. What percent support the proposal? Enter the percent with the percent sign.
questions.explanation: 45 divided by 75 is 0.60, so 60% of the sample supports the proposal.

questions.question: Which detail most directly helps readers judge whether a sample is representative?
options: How the sample was selected
The font used in the report
The color of the graph
Whether the title sounds exciting
questions.explanation: The selection method tells whether the sample had a fair chance to reflect the population.

questions.question: A survey asks only students using the library at lunch whether the library needs more seats. Which conclusion is most careful?
options: The data describe library users at lunch, but may not represent all students.
The data prove all students need more library seats.
The data cannot describe anyone at all.
The data prove that lunch should be cancelled.
questions.explanation: The sample is relevant to lunch library users but may be too narrow for a claim about all students.

questions.question: A neutral survey question avoids wording that pushes the respondent toward one answer.
questions.explanation: Neutral wording helps reduce response bias.

questions.question: Which question is worded most neutrally?
options: Which schedule do you prefer: current or later start?
Do you agree that our terrible current schedule should change?
Wouldn't a later start be much better?
Why is the current schedule the best?
questions.explanation: The first option presents choices without loaded words.

questions.question: In the claim "Most Grade 10 learners prefer digital reviewers," the smaller group actually surveyed is called the _____.
questions.explanation: The sample is the smaller group that is actually studied.

questions.question: A sample of 200 students comes only from one after-school robotics club. What is the best evaluation?
options: The sample is large, but it may still be biased because it comes from one club.
The sample must be representative because 200 is always enough.
The sample is random because clubs meet after school.
The sample proves the claim for every school in the country.
questions.explanation: A large sample from one narrow group can still fail to represent a wider population.

questions.question: A student surveyed 30 classmates from one section and claims, "All Grade 10 learners dislike oral reports." Explain why this claim is too strong.
questions.correctAnswer: The sample includes only one section, so it may not represent all Grade 10 learners. The conclusion should be limited to the surveyed classmates or supported by a broader sample.
questions.explanation: A strong answer identifies the mismatch between the narrow sample and the broad population claim.

questions.question: Which report gives the strongest evidence?
options: A random sample of 120 Grade 10 learners from all sections, with the exact question and date reported
A poll answered by 30 followers of one student's account
A survey of 50 students standing near one classroom door
A claim with no sample size or source
questions.explanation: The first report gives a fairer selection method, a clear sample size, and useful reporting details.

questions.question: Suggest one improvement for this sampling plan: Ask the first 20 students in the cafeteria about all students' preferred school event.
questions.correctAnswer: Randomly select students from different grade levels or sections instead of asking only the first 20 students in the cafeteria.
questions.explanation: The improvement should make the sample less dependent on one convenient location or group.

questions.question: A valid conclusion from a biased sample should usually do what?
options: State the result but clearly limit what population it describes
Ignore the sampling method
Claim the result proves the opinion of everyone
Remove the sample size
questions.explanation: When a sample is biased, the conclusion should be cautious and describe the limits of the evidence.

questions.question: In a random sample of 100 Grade 10 learners, 68 prefer digital reviewers. Write a careful conclusion about the claim "Most Grade 10 learners prefer digital reviewers."
questions.correctAnswer: In this random sample, 68% of Grade 10 learners preferred digital reviewers, so the data give reasonable evidence that most Grade 10 learners prefer digital reviewers.
questions.explanation: A good conclusion includes the sample statistic, notes the random sample, and connects cautiously to the population claim.
